items.followUp: What is the approximate value of g on the Moon in m s⁻²?

rubric.why: Award for the accepted value of gravitational acceleration on the Moon.
rubric.description: States the value of g on the Moon.
rubric.how: Look for approximately 1.6 m s⁻², 1.62 m s⁻², or one-sixth of the Earth’s value.

rubric.why: The value must be expressed with an appropriate unit.
rubric.description: Gives a correct unit.
rubric.how: Accept m s⁻² or N kg⁻¹.

modelAnswer: The value of g on the Moon is approximately 1.6 m s⁻² (about one-sixth of its value on Earth).

rubric.why: Award for identifying the quantity being defined and the relevant force.
rubric.description: Relates the joule to work done by a force.
rubric.how: The answer should define work done by a force.

rubric.why: One joule is defined by a one-newton force acting through one metre in its direction.
rubric.description: Gives the defining force and displacement.
rubric.how: Accept 1 N and 1 m, or their written names.

modelAnswer: One joule is the work done when a force of 1 N displaces a body through 1 m in the direction of the force.

items.followUp: Write two properties of a good thermometric liquid.

rubric.why: Uniform expansion is a desirable property of a thermometric liquid.
rubric.description: States that the liquid expands uniformly with temperature.
rubric.how: Accept uniform expansion or a high coefficient of expansion.

rubric.why: Any one of these is another standard property of a thermometric liquid.
rubric.description: States another valid property.
rubric.how: Accept that it does not wet or stick to glass, has a low freezing point, has a high boiling point, or is easily visible.

modelAnswer: A thermometric liquid expands uniformly with a change in temperature.
It does not wet or stick to the glass of the thermometer.

items.followUp: State the law of conservation of momentum and explain it for two bodies that collide.

rubric.why: The law states that total momentum remains constant in an isolated system.
rubric.description: States the law of conservation of momentum.
rubric.how: Look for total momentum before a collision equalling total momentum after it, or momentum being conserved in an isolated system.

rubric.why: This represents the combined momentum of the two spherical bodies before collision.
rubric.description: Gives the total initial momentum.
rubric.how: Accept the initial momentum expression or an equivalent verbal statement.

rubric.why: This represents the combined momentum of the two bodies after collision.
rubric.description: Gives the total final momentum.
rubric.how: Accept the final momentum expression or an equivalent verbal statement.

rubric.why: The example must show that the two bodies’ combined momentum is unchanged by the collision.
rubric.description: Equates total momentum before and after the collision.
rubric.how: Look for the conservation equation or a clear statement that the initial and final total momenta are equal.

modelAnswer: The law of conservation of momentum states that the total momentum of an isolated system remains constant if no external force acts on it.
Consider two spherical bodies of masses m₁ and m₂ moving with velocities u₁ and u₂ before collision.
Their total momentum before collision is m₁u₁ + m₂u₂.
If their velocities after collision are v₁ and v₂, their total momentum is m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
Thus, m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂: total momentum before collision equals total momentum after collision.

items.followUp: A car travels at a uniform speed of 54 km h⁻¹ for 8 s. Find the distance travelled.

rubric.why: The given speed must be converted to SI units before using the formula.
rubric.description: Converts the speed into m s⁻¹.
rubric.how: Accept 36 km h⁻¹ = 10 m s⁻¹.

rubric.why: The time is part of the given SI data.
rubric.description: Records the given time.
rubric.how: Look for t = 10 s.

rubric.why: Distance for uniform motion is speed multiplied by time.
rubric.description: Uses the correct formula.
rubric.how: Accept s = vt or an equivalent formula.

rubric.why: The substitution must use the SI speed and the given time.
rubric.description: Substitutes values into the formula.
rubric.how: Look for 10 m s⁻¹ multiplied by 10 s.

rubric.why: The correct distance is 100 m.
rubric.description: Gives the final distance with unit.
rubric.how: Accept 100 m.

modelAnswer: Given: v = 36 km h⁻¹ = 10 m s⁻¹; t = 10 s.
Formula: s = vt.
Substitution: s = (10 m s⁻¹)(10 s).
The train travels 100 m.

items.followUp: Why are precise clocks needed to measure the time taken by very fast events?

rubric.why: Some physical events occur over extremely brief intervals.
rubric.description: Identifies that some events have very short durations.
rubric.how: Look for a reference to very short or extremely small time intervals.

rubric.why: Precise measurement is needed to study or describe such events accurately.
rubric.description: Explains the need for measuring these intervals.
rubric.how: Accept a suitable example of a rapid event or a statement that measurement is needed for accurate study.

modelAnswer: Some physical processes, such as atomic vibrations or the motion of electrons, take place in extremely small intervals of time.
We need to measure these intervals accurately to study and describe such processes.

items.followUp: A runner covers 200 m in 25 s. Find the runner’s average speed.

rubric.why: Average speed is total distance divided by total time.
rubric.description: Uses the correct formula.
rubric.how: Accept v = s/t or average speed = distance/time.

rubric.why: The calculation gives 100 ÷ 12 = 8.33 m s⁻¹.
rubric.description: Calculates and states the average speed.
rubric.how: Accept 8.33 m s⁻¹ or 8.3 m s⁻¹.

modelAnswer: Given: distance = 100 m; time = 12 s.
Formula: average speed = distance ÷ time.
Substitution: average speed = 100 m ÷ 12 s = 8.33 m s⁻¹.
The sprinter’s average speed is 8.33 m s⁻¹.

items.followUp: Convert 5 m s⁻¹ into km h⁻¹.

rubric.why: The conversion uses 1 h = 3600 s and 1 km = 1000 m.
rubric.description: Shows the correct conversion factor.
rubric.how: Look for multiplying by 3600 and dividing by 1000, or the equivalent factor 3.6.

rubric.why: One metre per second equals 3.6 kilometres per hour.
rubric.description: Gives the converted value.
rubric.how: Accept 3.6 km h⁻¹.

modelAnswer: 1 m s⁻¹ = 3.6 km h⁻¹.
